items.title: Caedmon (fl. c. 7th c.)
items.meta: Old English / Anglo-Saxon Period · British & Irish Literature · 0 PYQs

fields.label: Writer Name
fields.value: Caedmon

fields.label: Life Dates
fields.value: fl. c. 7th c.

fields.label: L1 One-Line Flash Anchor
fields.value: Caedmon’s Hymn — foundational Old English religious poem associated with Caedmon.

fields.label: 2-Minute Simple Biography
fields.value: Caedmon is the earliest English poet whose name we know. Bede says he was a cowherd at the monastery of Whitby. He could not sing at a feast, then a dream taught him a hymn of creation. Abbess Hild tested the gift and received him as a monk. He was active in the late 7th century. No birth year is recorded.

fields.label: Why Important for UGC NET
fields.value: Unit 2 (Poetry). Questions ask who first sings Christian verse in English, and where Bede tells the story. They also test alliteration and the dream.

fields.label: Memory Tip & Exam Traps
fields.value: Whitby cowherd, dream of creation, nine lines, saved by Bede. | Caedmon’s Hymn — foundational Old English religious poem associated with Caedmon. | Known from Bede. Late seventh century.

items.title: Bede (673/674–735)
items.meta: Old English / Anglo-Saxon Period · British & Irish Literature · 2 PYQs

fields.label: Writer Name
fields.value: Bede

fields.label: L1 One-Line Flash Anchor
fields.value: Historia Ecclesiastica Gentis Anglorum (731) — Ecclesiastical History of the English People.

fields.label: 2-Minute Simple Biography
fields.value: Bede was a monk and scholar at the monasteries of Wearmouth and Jarrow. Reference works call him the Venerable Bede and the Father of English History. He was born in 672 or 673, on land of that monastery. At seven he was given to Abbot Benedict Biscop to be taught. He died at Jarrow in 735.

fields.label: Why Important for UGC NET
fields.value: Unit 4 (nonfictional prose). Questions ask the year 731, the five books, and the Latin language. They also ask how Caedmon enters the History.

fields.label: Memory Tip & Exam Traps
fields.value: Monk of Jarrow. History finished in 731. Died in 735. | Historia Ecclesiastica Gentis Anglorum (731) — Ecclesiastical History of the English People.

items.title: King Alfred the Great (849–899)
items.meta: Old English / Anglo-Saxon Period · British & Irish Literature · 0 PYQs

fields.label: Writer Name
fields.value: King Alfred the Great

fields.label: L1 One-Line Flash Anchor
fields.value: Alfredian learning revival; translation tradition including Gregory the Great’s Pastoral Care.

fields.label: 2-Minute Simple Biography
fields.value: Alfred the Great was king of Wessex from 871 to 899. Britannica gives his birth as 849, at Wantage. He fought the Danish armies and kept Wessex from falling. In the later years of peace he led a revival of learning in English. He died in 899.

fields.label: Why Important for UGC NET
fields.value: Unit 4 (nonfictional prose). Questions ask why he chose English, and which book carries the famous preface. They also separate the revival from one single title.

fields.label: Memory Tip & Exam Traps
fields.value: King 871 to 899. Preface to Pastoral Care about 890. English for needful books. | Alfredian learning revival; translation tradition including Gregory the Great’s Pastoral Care.

items.title: Cynewulf (probably 8th–9th c.)
items.meta: Old English / Anglo-Saxon Period · British & Irish Literature · 0 PYQs

fields.label: Writer Name
fields.value: Cynewulf

fields.label: Life Dates
fields.value: probably 8th–9th c.

fields.label: L1 One-Line Flash Anchor
fields.value: Elene; Juliana; The Fates of the Apostles; Christ II.

fields.label: 2-Minute Simple Biography
fields.value: Cynewulf is one of the few Old English poets who left his name. He wove it in runes at the end of four religious poems. The spelling of that name fits a date in the 9th century. His birth, his death, and his home are unknown. He wrote in an Anglian dialect, so he likely lived in Mercia or Northumbria. He knew Latin saints' lives and homilies.

fields.label: Why Important for UGC NET
fields.value: Unit 2 (Poetry). Questions match the four signed titles, the runes, and the two manuscripts. They also ask students not to add unsigned poems.

fields.label: Memory Tip & Exam Traps
fields.value: Four runic poems: Christ II, Elene, Juliana, Fates. Exeter and Vercelli. | Elene; Juliana; The Fates of the Apostles; Christ II.

items.title: Ælfric of Eynsham (c. 955–c. 1010)
items.meta: Old English / Anglo-Saxon Period · British & Irish Literature · 0 PYQs

fields.label: Writer Name
fields.value: Ælfric of Eynsham

fields.label: L1 One-Line Flash Anchor
fields.value: Catholic Homilies; Lives of Saints; Grammar.

fields.label: 2-Minute Simple Biography
fields.value: Aelfric of Eynsham was the leading writer of Old English prose in his time. He trained as a monk at Winchester under Bishop Aethelwold. In 987 he was sent to teach at Cerne Abbas. In 1005 he became the first abbot of Eynsham. He died about 1010. He is not the archbishop of Canterbury who shared his name.

fields.label: Why Important for UGC NET
fields.value: Unit 4 (nonfictional prose), with the Grammar also touching Unit 5 (language). Questions date the Homilies, the Grammar, and the Lives, and separate him from Archbishop Aelfric.

fields.label: Memory Tip & Exam Traps
fields.value: Cerne 987, Homilies about 990, Grammar 995, Lives 996, abbot 1005. | Catholic Homilies; Lives of Saints; Grammar.

fields.value: Beowulf — Old English heroic epic; Beowulf, Grendel, Grendel’s mother, the dragon; alliterative verse.

fields.label: 2-Minute Simple Biography
fields.value: These works come from unknown poets, not one named author. Beowulf and four shorter poems are Old English. Havelok the Dane is a later Middle English romance. No birth or death year can be fixed.

items.title: Wulfstan (d. c. 1014/16)
items.meta: Old English / Anglo-Saxon Period · British & Irish Literature · 0 PYQs

fields.label: Writer Name
fields.value: Wulfstan

fields.label: L1 One-Line Flash Anchor
fields.value: Sermo Lupi ad Anglos (“Sermon of the Wolf to the English”).

fields.label: 2-Minute Simple Biography
fields.value: Wulfstan was a bishop, law writer, and the fiercest preacher of late Old English prose. He became bishop of London in 996. In 1002 he became archbishop of York and bishop of Worcester. He kept Worcester until 1016 and York until his death. He died in 1023. He signed work as Lupus, the Latin word for wolf.

fields.label: Why Important for UGC NET
fields.value: Unit 4 (nonfictional prose). Questions ask the sermon title, the year 1014, and the meaning of Lupus. They also test his death in 1023 against that sermon year.

fields.label: Memory Tip & Exam Traps
fields.value: Wolf to the English, sermon about 1014, archbishop dies in 1023. | Sermo Lupi ad Anglos (“Sermon of the Wolf to the English”).

items.title: Dante Alighieri (1066–1340)

fields.label: Writer Name
fields.value: Dante Alighieri

fields.label: L1 One-Line Flash Anchor
fields.value: Italian. Completed around 1320. The book files him under European literature.

fields.label: 2-Minute Simple Biography
fields.value: Dante Alighieri was a poet of Florence, in Italy. He was born in 1265 and died in Ravenna in 1321. Florence banished him in 1302, and he never returned. His great poem, The Divine Comedy, is written in Italian.

fields.label: Why Important for UGC NET
fields.value: Unit 2 (Poetry, European literature). Questions test the three canticles, terza rima, Virgil and Beatrice, and the exile.

fields.label: Memory Tip & Exam Traps

items.title: Geoffrey of Monmouth (c. 1095–c. 1155)
items.meta: Early Middle English & Anglo-Norman · British & Irish Literature · 0 PYQs

fields.label: Writer Name
fields.value: Geoffrey of Monmouth

fields.label: L1 One-Line Flash Anchor
fields.value: Historia Regum Britanniae — major source for later Arthurian literary tradition.

fields.label: 2-Minute Simple Biography
fields.value: Geoffrey of Monmouth was a cleric and the Latin historian of legendary Britain. He is linked with Monmouth and with Oxford, where his name appears on charters from 1129. He was made bishop of Saint Asaph in 1151 and consecrated in 1152. The Welsh chronicles say he died in 1155. His birth is estimated near 1100.

fields.label: Why Important for UGC NET
fields.value: Unit 4 (nonfictional prose). Questions ask the Latin title, the date about 1136, and his role as a source for Arthur. They also ask students not to treat the book as fact.

fields.label: Memory Tip & Exam Traps
fields.value: History of the Kings of Britain, about 1136. Arthur, Leir, and Merlin. | Historia Regum Britanniae — major source for later Arthurian literary tradition.

items.title: Orm (fl. c. 1180)
items.meta: Early Middle English & Anglo-Norman · British & Irish Literature · 0 PYQs

fields.label: Writer Name
fields.value: Orm

fields.label: L1 One-Line Flash Anchor
fields.value: Ormulum — biblical/homiletic material; important for Middle English language history.

fields.label: 2-Minute Simple Biography
fields.value: Orm, also called Ormin, was an Augustinian canon in England. He wrote the Ormulum, Gospel homilies in English verse. He built a special spelling so priests could read the lines aloud. The only copy is his own manuscript.

fields.label: Why Important for UGC NET
fields.value: Unit 2 (Poetry). Questions test the spelling system and the Ormulum as early Middle English.

fields.label: Memory Tip & Exam Traps
fields.value: Ormulum about 1180, doubled consonants, Gospel homilies for Walter. | Ormulum — biblical/homiletic material; important for Middle English language history.

items.meta: Early Middle English & Anglo-Norman · British & Irish Literature · 1 PYQs

fields.label: Life Dates
fields.value: fl. late 12th–early 13th c.

fields.value: Brut — Middle English adaptation of Geoffrey of Monmouth; Arthurian chronicle.

fields.label: 2-Minute Simple Biography
fields.value: Layamon was a priest at Areley Kings in Worcestershire. He wrote the Brut, an early Middle English verse chronicle. The poem retells legendary British history from Brutus to the Saxons. It gives the first long English account of King Arthur.

fields.label: Why Important for UGC NET
fields.value: Unit 2 (Poetry). Questions test the Brut, the debt to Wace, and the early English Arthur.

fields.label: 2-Minute Simple Biography
fields.value: Julian of Norwich was an English anchoress and mystic. In May 1373, when she was about thirty, she received sixteen visions. She wrote a short account, then a much longer one. A will of 1416 still names an anchoress Julian in Norwich.

fields.label: Why Important for UGC NET
fields.value: Unit 4 (Non fictional prose). Questions test the 1373 visions, the two texts, and All shall be well.

fields.value: Margery Kempe was a married mystic from Bishop's Lynn, now King's Lynn. She could not write the book herself, so she dictated it. It is often called the earliest autobiography in English. She was still living in 1438.

items.title: Geoffrey Chaucer (c. 1340s–1400)
items.meta: The Age of Chaucer (Ricardian 14th Century) · British & Irish Literature · 23 PYQs

fields.label: Writer Name
fields.value: Geoffrey Chaucer

fields.label: L1 One-Line Flash Anchor
fields.value: The Canterbury Tales; Troilus and Criseyde; The Book of the Duchess; The House of Fame; The Parliament of Fowls; The Legend of Good Women.

fields.label: 2-Minute Simple Biography
fields.value: Geoffrey Chaucer was the greatest English poet of the Middle Ages. He was born in London between 1340 and 1345 and died on 25 October 1400. Before Chaucer, serious literature in England was written in Latin or French. He chose the London East Midland dialect and made it the standard literary English language.

fields.label: Why Important for UGC NET
fields.value: UGC NET tests Chaucer in almost every single paper under Unit II (Poetry). Questions focus on his three career periods (French, Italian, English), famous critical quotes about him, the exact pilgrim descriptions in the General Prologue, and the plots and sources of the 24 Canterbury Tales.

fields.label: Memory Tip & Exam Traps
fields.value: 3 Kings (Edward III, Richard II, Henry IV) + 3 Periods: French (Duchess 1369), Italian (House of Fame, Parliament of Foules, Troilus, Good Women), English (Canterbury Tales 1387). | The Canterbury Tales; Troilus and Criseyde; The Book of the Duchess; The House of Fame; The Parliament of Fowls; The Legend of Good Women.

fields.label: 2-Minute Simple Biography
fields.value: William Caxton was an English merchant, translator, and printer. He was born in Kent about 1422. In 1476 he set up the first printing press in England, at Westminster. He died about 1491 and was buried at St Margaret's, Westminster.

fields.label: Why Important for UGC NET
fields.value: Unit 4 (Non fictional prose). Questions test 1476, the 1485 Morte, and the prefaces on the English language.

fields.label: Memory Tip & Exam Traps

fields.label: L1 One-Line Flash Anchor
fields.value: The Bowge of Court (printed c. 1499–1500); Speke, Parrot composed c. 1521, printed posthumously in later collections.

fields.label: 2-Minute Simple Biography
fields.value: John Skelton was an English poet, priest, and tutor to Prince Henry. He was born about 1460 and died at Westminster on 21 June 1529. He wrote sharp satires, some against Cardinal Wolsey. His short rhyming lines are called Skeltonics.

fields.label: Why Important for UGC NET
fields.value: Unit 2 (Poetry). Questions test Skeltonics, the Wolsey satires, and the difference from rhyme royal.
